title: "God Can't Stand You"
hook: Does God really hate sinners and refuse even to look at them?
tldr: Reformed voices claim Adam died spiritually, his relationship with God broke, and God hates and cannot look at sinners. Genesis shows God seeking Adam and clothing him. Isaiah 59:2 is a temporary national rebuke, holiness means 'set apart', and Hebrew 'hate' (SANE) means reject or avoid. God draws near to imperfect people.
big_idea: God draws near to sinners; it is we who hide.

points.title: No 'spiritual death' in Genesis
points.text: Genesis 3 never mentions spiritual death. The only death the text suggests is losing access to the Tree of Life, which gave the ability to live forever.

points.title: God sought out Adam
points.text: Adam and Eve hid; God did not look away. He came looking for them, made garments for their shame, and kept speaking with their family outside the Garden.

points.title: God dwells among sinners
points.text: Noah, Abraham, Moses and David were flawed yet intimate with God, who dwelt among Israel in the midst of their uncleanness. Jesus ate with sinners.

points.title: Isaiah 59:2 is national and temporary
points.text: The 'separation' was a national rebuke: God withdrew earthly protection and blessings, while still speaking to Israel through a prophet. It says nothing of eternal separation.

points.title: Holy means set apart
points.text: In Hebrew, holy means set apart, consecrated, devoted, expressing covenant commitment. It does not mean God cannot bear the presence of sinners.

points.title: Biblical 'hate' means reject
points.text: The Hebrew SANE means reject, avoid or ignore, as in 'Esau I have hated' and 'hate father and mother'. In Psalm 5:5 God rejects idolaters, yet loves even the worst sinners.

sections.summary: A GotQuestions article on why we suffer for Adam's sin cites Romans 5:12 and quietly adds two doctrines: Adam immediately died spiritually, and his relationship with God was broken. In this Augustinian-Calvinist view everyone is born spiritually dead, damned before their first breath, with God too upset for relationship. Creation.com agrees: we are all born in sin, so our default destination by original sin is hell, not heaven.

The phrase is vague and usually means total depravity and destined damnation, a conclusion from the TULIP doctrine, not the text. Genesis 3 lists consequences but no spiritual death. Adam and Eve had the Tree of Life; after eating from the Tree of Knowledge, God fulfilled his warning of death by revoking access to it. Living forever came from eating that tree, not inherent nature. That loss is the only death the text suggests.

sections.h: Was Adam's relationship with God broken?
sections.summary: If God cannot look at sinners, he cannot be near them, hates them, and must send all humanity to hellfire. R.C. Sproul called 'God hates the sin but loves the sinner' nonsense. But Genesis shows Adam and Eve hiding, not God turning away. God sought them out and made garments for their shame. Did he do it with eyes closed? They were banished from the Garden, not his presence; God kept engaging their family in Genesis 4.

Salvation must be grace, since finite efforts cannot earn it, but that does not mean God hates our imperfections. God may despise sin, yet mistakes build character; he watches our efforts to overcome evil more than the sins. David sinned, bore consequences, repented and worshipped. Baptism does not make us sinless; Paul called himself the worst of sinners. Jesus covers our sins, freeing us from fear of being hated by God.

Noah, Abraham, Moses and David were great sinners yet intimate with God. God dwelt among a nation of sinners, his tent in the midst of their uncleanness. What loving parent would torture children for flaws? Good parents redeem, teach, discipline and restore. Jesus came to seek sinners, eating with and blessing them, and spoke of a compassionate, protective Father who reaches out to deliver his sinful children.

Defenders cite 'your eyes are too pure to look on evil' and 'your iniquities have separated you from your God'. In Habakkuk's Hebrew parallelism, 'look on' parallels 'tolerate': God is too holy to ignore the evil in the nation. It is a figure of speech, not God's eyes avoiding evil people; otherwise Job, where God speaks with Satan, would conflict. Paul Washer and GotQuestions read Isaiah 59:2 as eternal separation from God.

Isaiah 59:2 is eisegesis when read as eternal separation. First, it rebukes the nation; Israel was always sinful yet kept a national relationship, and nations cannot be eternally separated in hellfire. Second, the separation is a temporary withdrawal of physical protection and blessings, as Deuteronomy warns. Third, God is actively talking to Israel, so there is no cut-off. Fourth, Isaiah, a man of unclean lips, saw God and spoke for him.

God answers Israel's question about why blessings and protection vanished. He does not disappear but pursues Israel through prophets, explaining consequences: discipline and restoration from a loving Parent. Deuteronomy 28 warned he would not protect a disobedient Israel from evil; that is the separation (59:1). If God cut off Israel, it would have vanished, but he promised never to leave or forsake them. Like the Prodigal Son's father, it is we who distance ourselves.

Psalm 99:5 says he is holy. Holy evokes halos today, but in Hebrew it means set apart, unique; the seventh day was holy for a special purpose, not because other days were bad. Peter Gentry: holy means consecrated or devoted, expressing covenant commitment. If holiness barred sinners, God's appearances, promises and the Son living among sinners would be impossible, and an omnipresent God is always present, sustaining the universe.

sections.h: Holiness like a sterile operating room
sections.summary: Because God is holy, the places he inhabits must be distinct. Like a sterilized surgical room, his dwelling in Israel's camp had to be cleansed when defiled, with the blood of offerings acting as a spiritual antiseptic. Unlike restrictive religious holiness, the holy Jesus touched, loved and cared for sinners. Holiness does not block relationship; it reveals a love so deep God became one of us.

John Piper, citing Psalm 5:5, said God does hate sinners; Mark Driscoll preached that God hates who you are; David Platt quoted Psalm 5:5-6. The ECT logic: everyone sins, God hates sinners and must separate from them, so he hates and damns everyone, even newborns and toddlers. This seems to clash with John 3:16, where 'world' means its people: God so loved the sinners.

Biblical Hebrew's limited vocabulary gives words broad, context-dependent meanings that evolve. Mitchell Dahood reads Psalm 5 as a repudiation of false gods when accused of idolatry; VanGemeren sees God distinguishing himself from deities that mixed good and evil. So the psalm says God hates idol worshippers, pagans who did not just lie about an evening dress but burned their babies as sacrifices. Yet this is not the main misuse.

English 'hate' evokes violence and wrath; preachers misread Hebrew through translation, sometimes to support an agenda. The Hebrew SANE means reject, avoid, deny or ignore; the Ancient Hebrew Lexicon pictures a thorn seed you turn to avoid. In Romans 9:10-13, 'Esau I have hated' means God rejected Esau and elected Jacob. A wife who hates her husband turns indifferent and leaves; you fight for what you cherish.

'No one ever hated their own body' means no one ignores it; we drink when thirsty even if we emotionally dislike ourselves, as the author did as a chubby kid with zits. Luke 14:26's 'hate father and mother' must mean choose Jesus over them, since we must love even enemies; the author lived this when his Jewish mother demanded he reject Jesus. God rejects idols and idolaters, yet loves the greatest sinners.

God did not make humanity all-knowing, all-wise and immortal like himself, but limited and finite. There is a vast gap between his perfection and our fallibility, limited abilities, restricted knowledge and need to survive. Yet fundamentalism and ECT insist God must torture us eternally because of the very gap between how he is and how he made us. That is neither sensible, just nor ethical.

steps.note: The first premise of the ECT reading.

steps.label: Everyone sins
steps.note: Including, on this view, every newborn and toddler.

steps.label: God hates sinners
steps.note: Breaks here: SANE means reject or avoid, and Psalm 5 targets idolaters.

steps.label: God must separate from sinners
steps.note: Breaks again: God dwelt amid Israel's uncleanness and Jesus ate with sinners.

steps.label: So all are damned
steps.note: Contradicts John 3:16: God so loved the world, its sinners.

mythfact.myth: God cannot even look at sinners.
mythfact.fact: Adam and Eve hid from God; God sought them, clothed them, and dwelt among Israel in the midst of their uncleanness.

mythfact.myth: Isaiah 59:2 teaches eternal separation from God.
mythfact.fact: It is a national rebuke about God temporarily withdrawing earthly protection, spoken through a prophet while God was actively talking to Israel.

mythfact.myth: 'Esau I have hated' shows God's violent loathing of individuals.
mythfact.fact: Hebrew SANE means reject or avoid; God rejected Esau and elected Jacob, not wishing Esau a violent death.

mythfact.myth: Holiness means God must keep away from the impure.
mythfact.fact: Holy means set apart and devoted in covenant commitment; the holy Jesus touched, loved and cared for sinners.

quiz.q: According to Genesis, what is the only 'death' Adam and Eve's sin brought?
options: Loss of access to the Tree of Life
quiz.why: Living forever came from eating the Tree of Life; revoking access fulfilled God's warning. Genesis 3 never mentions spiritual death.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word SANE, translated 'hate', mean?
quiz.why: SANE is used for rejecting or avoiding, as in God rejecting Esau and electing Jacob.

quiz.q: Why is Isaiah 59:2 not about eternal separation?
options: It is a national rebuke about temporarily lost protection
quiz.why: It addresses the nation, concerns earthly blessings and protection, and God is actively speaking to Israel through a prophet.

reflect: When you fail, do you picture God turning away from you, or coming to look for you as he did in Eden?
